newsitem.title: INDIA: UK's Major basks in warm Indian welcome.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major basks in warm Indian welcome.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major basked in the praise of India's media on Friday on the second day of his visit to South Asia, but at home the prospect of a minority government loomed.
Major's visit was dubbed a success by India's media, which praised him for his charm and commitment to trade with India.
"There was cricket fever, film fever, football fever, and now there is a Major fever," Calcutta's Telegraph newspaper said in a front-page story.
Trade was the focus of Major's week-long tour of the subcontinent, which would also take him to Bangladesh and Pakistan.

One company, British Telecommunications Plc, was poised to announce an important new Indian venture on Friday, adding to a list of long-term contracts Major said he is keen to foster, executives said.
But domestic politics was never far away on Major's last scheduled foreign trip before a general election which must be held by May at the latest.
Major, lagging the opposition Labour Party by around 20 points in opinion polls, has already lost his overall majority in parliament.

But the prospect of a minority government loomed after Major's ruling Conservatives announced on Thursday it would call a by-election in the Conservative seat of Wirral South, left vacant by the death of its member of parliament, Barry Porter.
The Conservatives had been expected to try to avoid calling the by-election to avoid an embarrassing defeat.

Losing the seat would leave Major's ruling Conservatives in an overall minority of one, although they would still have around 50 seats more than Labour and could soldier on with the support of northern Irish MPs.
But under pressure, the ruling party decided to go ahead in a move which commentators said made a March general election less likely.
Major, who needs time to make inroads on Labour's poll lead, was now expected to go to the country in either April or May.

Major has dismissed suggestions by senior Conservatives that he should have stayed at home to continue the election fight rather than taking time out for a long foreign trip. Major, who was counting on Britian's booming economy to win him back voters, argued "the business of government must go on."
He spent some of his time in India sending clear signals to the Indian community at home, who could hold the key to a handful of marginal parliamentary seats.
Major on Thursday in a speech to thousands of Indian businessmen praised Britain's Indian community for its strong family values -- a phrase closely linked with the ruling Conservative party.
Major enjoyed an ecstatic reception on his public appearances during his visit to Calcutta on Thursday, the first time a serving British prime minister had visited the city.
Major was serenaded by a children's band and brightly clad young dancing girls on his visit to a Calcutta slum which has received British aid to improve basic amenities.
And at an evening reception for businessmen and leading figures from industry, Major was mobbed.
Major toured British projects in Calcutta on Friday morning before holding talks with Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on the plane taking the two men to Bangalore in southern India.
Major was scheduled to visit factories and companies with British links in Bangalore before leaving on Friday night for Bangladesh.
